title: Skipping the Zeros in Diffusion Models for Sparse Data Generation
claim: Dense baselines corrupt exact-zero sparsity patterns with spurious non-zeros, while our sparse-aware model preserves clean patterns matching real data.
layout: 5 stacked rows of 8 samples, top-to-bottom, row labels left, bracket
description: A stacked comparison of MNIST samples, with five horizontal black-bordered strips. Row labels sit on the left in large text. The top row, 'Original images', shows eight grayscale handwritten digits (2 3 1 9 6 0 9 2) on black. A vertical bracket labelled 'Sparsity patterns' groups the other four rows. 'Ground truth' shows binary white-on-black masks of the same digits. The 'DDPM' and 'LDM' rows are eight square masks each. They are mostly white and noisy, with scattered black speckles and spurious non-zero pixels that fill the background. The final row, 'SED (ours)', shows clean white-on-black digit masks (6 3 5 3 9 5 0 7) with a pure black background, like the ground truth. The eye goes first to the contrast between the noisy white baseline rows and the clean black SED row.
caption: Sparsity preservation on MNIST. While dense models (DDPM, LDM) fail to preserve exact zeros and introduce spurious non-zero entries, the proposed Sparsity-Exploiting Diffusion (SED) model preserves sparsity patterns closely aligned with the ground truth.
abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) excel on dense continuous data, but are not designed for sparse continuous data. They do not model exact zeros that represent the deliberate absence of a signal. As a result, they erase sparsity patterns and perform unnecessary computation on mostly zero entries. With Sparsity-Exploiting Diffusion (SED), we model only non-zero values, preserving sparsity. SED delivers computational savings while maintaining or improving generation quality by skipping zeros during training and inference. Across physics and biology benchmarks, SED matches or surpasses conventional DMs and domain-specific baselines, while vision experiments provide intuitive insights into the limitations of dense DMs and the benefits of SED.
